blocks.text: For to a dog a dog seems the most beautiful thing, and an ox to an ox, an ass to an ass, a pig to a pig. And Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods book 1: Do you think there is any beast on land or sea that does not take the greatest delight in a beast of its own kind? If it were not so, why would a bull not long to touch a mare, or a stallion a cow? Or do you suppose that an eagle, or a lion, or a dolphin prefers any shape to its own? So the Hebrews and the Arabs talk nonsense when they keep saying that the raven shrinks from its newly hatched chicks because they are wonderfully ugly. For if τὰ κορακίδια [ta korakidia] look vile to us, it does not follow that they look vile also to their parents, who view them with other eyes. And indeed, although these fables were invented solely to explain Scripture, they in no way agree with the words of Scripture. For Job does not say that the chicks of the ravens cry to God in the nest, but when they wander and stray about for lack of food. The subject, therefore, is chicks that have already left the nest. For that chicks should wander here and there within the nest itself, as Gregory says, cannot be conceived; the narrowness of a nest does not allow such wandering of the chicks. Nor in fact does the raven neglect its young while they are in the nest; rather, once they are fully reared and able to fly, it drives them from the nest, so that thereafter they may provide for themselves. The Philosopher, Hist. book 9, ch. 31: Οἱ δὲ κόρακες τοὺς ἑαυτῶν νεοττοὺς, ὅταν οἷοί τ᾽ ὦσιν ἤδη πέτεσθαι, τὸ μὲν πρῶτον ἐκβάλλουσιν, [II, 799] ὕστερον δὲ καὶ ἐκ τοῦ τόπου ἐκδιώκουσι· [Hoi de korakes tous heautōn neottous, hotan hoioi t᾽ ōsin ēdē petesthai, to men prōton ekballousin, hysteron de kai ek tou topou ekdiōkousi] But ravens, when their chicks are now able to fly, first cast them out of the nest, then drive them out of the whole district. Pliny, book 10, ch. 12, on the crow: This bird alone even feeds its chicks for some time after they can fly. All the others of the same kind drive their chicks from the nests and force them to fly, as do the ravens too, which drive each of their young, once strong, farther away. Aelian, On Animals book 2, ch. 49: Τούς γε μὴν νεοττοὺς τοὺς ἐκτραφέντας διώκουσι, καὶ τῆς ἑαυτῶν ἕκαστος καλιᾶς φυγάδας ἀποφαίνουσιν ὑπὲρ ὅτου τροφὰς μαστεύουσι. [Tous ge mēn neottous tous ektraphentas diōkousi, kai tēs heautōn hekastos kalias phygadas apophainousin hyper hotou trophas masteuousi.] Their chicks, indeed, once reared, they chase away; and each drives them from its nest, for which reason the chicks thereafter seek their own food. It is only when the chicks have been cast out in this way, then, that there happens [col. 208] what the sacred writer relates: that, wandering for lack of food, they as it were cry to God. For since they are not yet at full strength, nor in the perfect vigour of their age, and have not yet grown used to procuring food for themselves by their own effort and industry, they are utterly at a loss, croak loudly, and fill the air with plaintive cries, as though complaining to God of their parents' ἀστοργία [astorgia]. And in these straits God comes to their aid, not by miraculously producing flies and gnats that thrust themselves of their own accord into their mouths, but by suggesting to them what must be done and how to provide against pressing hunger, so that they do not perish of starvation. Thus the same thing happens here to the chicks of ravens as to the whelps of lions, which, deserted by their mother, lack and suffer hunger, Psal. XXXIV, 11, and roar after their prey, as though seeking their food from God, Psal. CIV, 21. And God satisfies them, Iob. XXXIX, 1 (var. XXXVIII, 39). Yet one need not trouble much over why this is attributed to the chicks of ravens rather than to the ravens themselves, since Christ said it of ravens too, Luc. XII, 24: Consider the ravens, which neither sow etc. and yet God feeds them. Nor was there any reason for the Arabic translator to render ravens as فراخا الغربان [firākhā al-ghirbān] chicks of ravens. For a translator may not change anything in the words of the sacred text unless necessity compels him, and here no such necessity appears, since Christ says nothing of ravens that does not suit the whole species. Consider, he says, the ravens, which neither sow nor reap, which have neither storeroom nor barn, and yet God feeds them. This is as true of the parents as of the chicks: neither sows or reaps; neither has storerooms or barns. Finally, God provides for both alike. Indeed, Christ applies these same words to all birds, Matth. VI, 26: Consider, he says, the birds of the air, which neither sow nor reap etc. But what he asserts there of birds in general he narrows, Matth. X, 29, to sparrows, which, though very cheap and sold two for a farthing, God nevertheless does not judge unworthy of his care. And in Luc. XII, 24 he extends the same to ravens too, which, ugly birds though they are, harsh of voice and of ill omen, he nevertheless does not disdain to feed. So nothing peculiar is attributed here to ravens or to the chicks of ravens. Rather, they, like the sparrows, are expressly mentioned among the other birds, to make clear that God's providence not only cares for birds in general, but extends even to the cheapest and most despised of them, [II, 800] so that men, and faithful men above all, may conclude the more surely that they are in God's care: what he so kindly grants to little creatures of the lowest order, he will not deny to those by whom he is worshipped and invoked. Having explained these things thus, I will not conceal that in Servius, in his Notes on book 1 of the Georgics, one reads this: Pliny in his Natural History says that ravens are forgetful and for the most part do not return to their nests at all; but by a certain provision of nature they gather at their nests things that can produce worms, by which their abandoned chicks are sometimes fed. Hence it may seem that the fable we have refuted can be confirmed by the authority of Pliny. But there is no reason for this to trouble anyone. For Servius either deceives or is deceived, since nothing of the kind is read either in Pliny or in any of the philosophers who preceded the age of Servius. So this is a mere dream from the ivory gate, of the sort that learned men have already observed slipped from him in large numbers.
